story: An elderly Brahmin named Vishnusharma was tasked with teaching the principles of good governance and wise conduct to three ignorant princes, sons of King Amarasakti of Mahilaropya. He did so through five interlinked books of animal fables. In the first book, a jackal minister named Damanaka, unemployed in a lion king's court, conspired with his sidekick Karataka to break apart close friendships and alliances among the animals, illustrating how trust is lost. The second book followed four weak animals—a crow, a mouse, a turtle, and a deer—who, by working together and supporting one another, escaped every threat and prospered, showing that cooperation among the weak can achieve what strength alone cannot. The third book told of war between crows and owls: the crow king heeded the wise counsel of his advisor, while the owl king ignored his own advisor, and so the crows triumphed. This book also told of an old man who married a young woman who despised him; when a thief entered their home one night, she embraced her husband from fear, delighting him so much that he thanked the thief and offered him anything he wished. The fourth and fifth books, shorter and focused on human folly, warned against haste. One fable told of a woman who left her child with a loyal mongoose; finding blood on its mouth upon her return, she killed it in anger, only to discover it had saved her child from a snake, and she grieved her hasty act.
